title: An Indus seal as a made object
summary: An Indus seal can be examined as a worked material before anyone attempts to explain its signs.

body.text: A seal is easily reduced to its picture: an animal, a row of signs, an intriguing composition. Yet its surface also belongs to a manufactured object. Before asking what an inscription means, we can ask what was cut, what was heated and which observations belong to this particular specimen. That change of attention brings an otherwise anonymous maker into view without inventing a name or translating an unread text.

Harappa's published photographic record includes an instructive contrast. Jonathan Mark Kenoyer identifies an unfired rectangular steatite seal beside a fired and glazed example, both assigned to the later Harappa Phase. The same commentary distinguishes another fired and glazed seal from the preceding phase. These are not interchangeable illustrations of one timeless technique: their material condition and archaeological dating are part of the evidence.
From soft stone to finished surface

Kenoyer's workshop study explains that steatite could be shaped while relatively soft and subsequently transformed by high-temperature firing. This gives the finished object a history that its present hardness alone does not reveal. The study also concerns faience, a different manufactured material; a pale or glazed appearance therefore should not replace an actual material identification.

Imagine documenting a seal for an exhibition. A face-on photograph records the composition, but a second view of its edge could help readers understand thickness and damage. A scale prevents a small carving from being mentally enlarged into a monumental relief. A material description tells us something that colour reproduction cannot. These are different kinds of information, and none needs to compete with the visual pleasure of the image.

An individual button seal provides a useful anchor. The Harappa Archaeological Research Project records H2000-4432/2174-3 from the Trench 54 area as fired steatite bearing four concentric-circle designs. Keeping that identifier with the image allows an editor to distinguish this find from superficially similar pieces. A generic caption such as “ancient seal” would discard that connection.
Making, use and meaning are different questions

Manufacturing evidence does not automatically establish how long a seal was used, who controlled it or what every mark signified. A proposed sequence of carving and firing is a statement about production. A claim about an owner's occupation requires another kind of support. An interpretation of the signs requires something different again. The confidence attached to one conclusion cannot simply be transferred to the others.

For a visitor, the most rewarding exercise is to keep those questions alongside one another. What can the photograph show? What has an excavator recorded? What has a materials specialist established? What remains an interpretation? Looking this way does not make the object less evocative. It replaces an imagined certainty with a more tangible achievement: a person selected a material and made a small surface capable of carrying an exceptionally deliberate design.

title: Standardised weights and the evidence of measurement
summary: Indus weights reveal relationships between measured quantities, but they are not a deciphered price list or a known currency.

body.text: A group of stone cubes can look modest beside a sculpture or seal. Its importance emerges when the pieces are measured together. The question is not simply how heavy each one is, but whether their masses form a patterned relationship. That relationship is evidence of a practice shared by makers and users, even when the words they used for its units are unavailable.

The published display of Indus weights on Harappa.com identifies banded chert among their materials and describes a sequence of smaller units increasing by doubling. The same page also corrects a misleading visual impression: a conical shell object included in the photograph is not a weight. Even a carefully arranged museum group must therefore be read with its catalogue rather than treated as a self-explanatory set.
A system is more than a neat row

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's study of Harappan measurement revisits older claims that apparent uniformity demonstrated unusually rigid civic control. Its investigation of measured objects instead asks about standardisation alongside variation. This is a productive distinction. Repeated proportions can show that people recognised a convention; they do not, by themselves, identify the institution that maintained it or explain how disagreements were settled.

Consider a hypothetical group with masses close to one, two, four and eight units. The pattern would be more persuasive than a collection whose values have no evident relationship. But an honest presentation would also show actual measurements, missing pieces and departures from the pattern. Rounding every value until it fits the proposed sequence would conceal the very evidence being tested.

There is a further difference between mass and value. A weight can help measure a material, but it does not tell us its price. A measured quantity of one substance need not exchange for the same quantity of another. Calling a stone weight a coin, or assigning it a modern currency equivalent, would introduce a financial system that the object has not established.
What a useful label should preserve

For an individual piece, readers need the material identification, recorded mass, dimensions, find context and collection number. For an assemblage, they also need to know whether the objects were excavated together or assembled for comparison. A display can bring pieces from different places into a visually convincing sequence; that arrangement is an editorial decision, not necessarily an ancient arrangement recovered intact.

This makes weights particularly good objects for learning how archaeological reasoning works. A proposal becomes stronger when another reader can inspect the observations behind it. A tidy diagram is helpful only if it leaves that route open. The small stone cube then becomes more than a symbol of an “advanced civilisation.” It introduces a specific problem: how people made quantities comparable across transactions, work and distance, and how much of that agreement can still be reconstructed from surviving things.

title: A carnelian bead’s long production journey
summary: Carnelian beads preserve evidence of shaping, drilling and finishing, while workshop comparisons reveal choices rather than one uniform production line.

body.text: A carnelian bead is a small object with a demanding internal problem: a hole must pass through stone without destroying the form around it. Its outside is what a wearer displays, but the perforation can be equally important to an archaeologist. A complete account therefore considers both the attractive finished surface and the less visible labour that made the bead usable.

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's study of Indus bead technology makes Chanhudaro in Sindh a particularly valuable example. The workshop assemblage included roughly finished short beads as well as carefully shaped and polished long carnelian examples made with specialised drills. Different levels of finishing occurred within one production setting. It would be misleading to turn every rough bead into evidence of an incompetent maker or an earlier stage of civilisation.
Following a sequence without inventing a worker

Raw material, shaping, perforation, finishing and use are separate questions. A proposed production sequence should explain which marks support each step. It should also allow for an object that left manufacture without being worn, or one whose comparatively rough finish was acceptable to its user. “Finished” is not necessarily a synonym for the smoothest object in a modern display case.

Kenoyer discusses the significance of wear inside perforations and the absence of such wear in the Chanhudaro examples he examined. These observations help distinguish production history from later use. They do not supply an owner's identity or the price paid for an ornament. The distinction matters because a beautifully made bead is often invited to carry a complete social biography that its surviving evidence cannot support.

An ethnographic study of carnelian production at Khambhat in India offers a different kind of comparison. It documents connected tasks and specialised working arrangements in a living industry. Such research can help archaeologists ask better questions about manufacturing waste and the organisation of labour. It is not a licence to transfer a modern worker's tools, contracts or family structure unchanged into an Indus workshop.
The journey is not a single arrow

An exhibition map might draw an elegant line from a stone source to a workshop and then to a distant settlement. Each connection nevertheless needs its own evidence. Finding a finished bead at the destination does not identify every stop along the way. Nor does a shared colour prove that two stones came from the same deposit. A responsible diagram can distinguish a demonstrated connection from a suggested route.

The bead's long journey is consequently best approached as a set of connected investigations. Where did its material originate? Which operations are visible? Was it used, repaired or restrung? Where was it finally deposited? These questions preserve the fascination of movement while resisting an invented travel story. They also restore attention to the maker's practical choices: the alignment of a hole, the treatment of a surface and the decision that this particular piece was ready to leave the workshop.

title: Faience is not simply blue stone
summary: Indus faience was a deliberately manufactured material, not merely a blue stone. Workshop evidence makes its technical character visible.

body.text: Blue-green colour can make an ancient bead seem straightforward: an attractive stone, selected and polished. Faience asks us to reconsider that first impression. Its appearance results from making a material as well as shaping an object. Understanding the distinction changes the kind of skill we recognise and the questions we ask of a museum label.

In his report on Harappa's Mound E workshop, Jonathan Mark Kenoyer describes faience manufacture involving processed quartz, colouring materials and high-temperature firing. He distinguishes this from steatite, a stone that could be carved and subsequently fired. The workshop investigated in the 2000–2001 excavations contained evidence for both industries. Their association does not make the two materials identical.
Colour is an observation, not an identification

A visitor can describe a blue-green surface without knowing its composition. A catalogue's material identification goes further, and ideally rests on specialist examination. Keeping those two statements separate is important when a photograph has altered the apparent colour, when a surface has changed in burial or when an old label uses terminology differently from a modern technical report.

The practical consequence is simple. A story about faience should not illustrate itself with any blue object that happens to be available. The selected object needs a recorded identification. If the record says steatite, it cannot silently become faience because the layout would benefit from another photograph. A visually coherent display must remain a materially accurate one.

The workshop study gives manufacturing debris and unfinished pieces a role alongside completed ornaments. For interpretation, this reverses a familiar hierarchy: the less spectacular fragment may help answer a question that the intact object leaves open. A finished surface presents a successful outcome. Material left during production can make the operations behind that outcome easier to investigate.
A workshop is an argument assembled from evidence

Calling an excavated area a workshop is more informative when the explanation identifies the relevant finds and their relationships. One isolated ornament would not, on its own, demonstrate local manufacture. A claim about production asks whether the assemblage includes convincing traces of making and whether the context supports their association. The reasoning should remain visible rather than being compressed into a colourful reconstruction of workers at a furnace.

It is equally important not to make this a recipe. An archaeological account of a high-temperature process is not an instruction to reproduce it at home, and a modern demonstration should identify its own materials and adaptations. Replication can test a proposal, but a successful modern object does not prove that every ancient maker followed the same procedure.

Faience rewards this slower attention because it complicates the boundary between “natural” material and crafted appearance. The object is not less accomplished once its colour is explained. Its beauty becomes connected to controlled transformations, accumulated knowledge and decisions whose material consequences survive even when the maker's own explanation does not.

title: Shell bangles and connections to the coast
summary: Shell bangles connect inland archaeological finds to marine materials, but workshop waste is needed to understand where and how they were made.

body.text: A pale curved fragment from an inland settlement may preserve a connection to the sea. Yet the connection is not a complete itinerary. A shell bangle can demonstrate the use of marine material without revealing whether a whole shell, a partly worked ring or a finished ornament travelled to the place where it was found. Those alternatives imply different distributions of labour.

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's study of Indus shell industries identifies several species used in ornament production. It also explains a limitation that is easy to overlook: a small finished fragment may have lost the anatomical features needed for a confident species identification. The surviving object can therefore be recognisably shell while its more precise biological attribution remains uncertain.
Looking at what was cut away

The study reconstructs bangle manufacture using working traces and discarded pieces. Saw cuts, shell anatomy and unfinished forms help distinguish stages that a polished ring can conceal. Kenoyer's research at Balakot adds a coastal production context to the broader comparison. Together these investigations encourage us to treat manufacturing waste as evidence, not merely as the unattractive remainder of a collection.

Suppose a hypothetical inland excavation yields only finished bangles. It would be reasonable to ask how the ornaments arrived, but premature to announce a local bangle factory. If another context contains consistently related blanks and cutting waste, the production question changes. The importance lies in the combination of finds and their recorded setting, not in the simple number of attractive objects recovered.

This distinction also changes how we imagine exchange. A map line from coast to city is a summary of a relationship, not necessarily a direct journey by one merchant. Material could have changed hands, form and value along the way. Unless a particular route is independently documented, an illustration should leave the intermediate stages open rather than give them invented certainty.
Ornament does not explain its wearer

A bangle's shape invites comparison with objects worn today. Comparison can make an unfamiliar fragment intelligible, but it cannot by itself establish an ancient wearer's marital status, community or ritual obligations. Contemporary meanings belong to particular people and settings. They should not be projected backwards simply because both objects encircle a wrist.

For an exhibition, a useful arrangement might place an accurately identified finished fragment beside a documented working piece and a diagram of the relevant shell anatomy. The purpose would not be to reconstruct a universal Indus workshop, but to make one supported manufacturing argument understandable. Each object would retain its own location, period and collection identifier.

Shell bangles thus open two different histories. One concerns the movement of material between marine environments and inland settlements. The other concerns skilled transformation: understanding an irregular natural form well enough to cut a desired object from it. Keeping both in view gives the fragment more depth than either an isolated jewellery label or a sweeping claim about ancient trade can provide.

title: Copper alloy objects: why composition matters
summary: A copper-coloured object is not a chemical analysis. Composition helps distinguish metal choices while leaving questions about intention and sourcing open.

body.text: “Bronze” can sound like a complete explanation of an ancient metal object. In fact, it may conceal several questions. What elements were measured? How was the object made? Did its composition result from a deliberate recipe, the character of the raw material, or the reuse of earlier metal? An artefact's outline does not answer all of these at once.

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer and Heather M.-L. Miller's review of Indus metal technologies makes this uncertainty explicit. Their survey discusses differing thresholds used to classify copper alloys and cautions that low concentrations of additional elements do not necessarily demonstrate intentional alloying. It also notes that similarly shaped objects could have different compositions. Form and chemistry are related avenues of investigation, not substitutes for each other.
A description and a result

A catalogue should distinguish an identification supported by analysis from one inherited from an older description. “Copper alloy” can be a useful cautious term where the exact composition is not established. It is less dramatic than a specific metallurgical claim, but more informative than a precision the available record cannot justify.

Imagine two objects of the same shape in adjacent cases. One has a published laboratory result; the other has only an early catalogue entry. Writing identical confident captions would erase that difference in knowledge. A better interpretation explains why the first identification is more specific and what would be required to investigate the second. Visitors can then understand uncertainty as a feature of the evidence, rather than as an omission to disguise.

The review also points to weaknesses in the available sample and inconsistencies between earlier investigations. These qualifications matter when someone tries to turn a handful of analyses into a claim about an entire civilisation. A dataset may illuminate the objects examined without representing every workshop, region or period equally well.
Chemistry is not a biography

Even a reliable composition does not name a maker or identify every movement of the material. An explanation of sourcing needs comparisons and context beyond the finished object's appearance. Likewise, a difference between two objects need not mean that one craftsperson was more capable. Before ranking the work, we would need to know what each maker or user was trying to achieve.

This approach changes the way technological sophistication is discussed. Rather than placing objects on a simple ladder from crude to advanced, it asks which practical choices can be demonstrated. The result may be a more complicated history, but it is also more respectful of craft: it does not assume that every material decision was directed towards a single modern ideal.

The most useful museum encounter therefore moves between scales. The whole object offers clues about shape and handling. Its catalogue establishes context and identity. A specialist report addresses questions that the eye alone cannot settle. Keeping those layers connected lets an apparently familiar metal object remain an active piece of evidence, rather than a label whose certainty exceeds what has actually been tested.

title: Terracotta figurines without invented identities
summary: Terracotta figurines invite stories, but observation, archaeological context and changing interpretations should come before invented identities.

body.text: A small clay figure seems to ask for a name. Goddess, ruler, child, animal companion: familiar identities can make an object immediately memorable. They can also conceal how little is known about its original use. The first task is not to suppress imagination, but to prevent a plausible story from replacing the surviving evidence.

Two early photographs from Harappa make the problem unusually visible. The archival images identified as ASI 416/86 and 423/86 show a terracotta human head and a humped bull. In one photograph the head was placed upside down; the other corrects its orientation. Before any larger interpretation, there was a basic problem of how to look at the fragment.
Begin with what can be checked

A description can record the surviving headgear, applied details, breaks and the relationship between separate parts. These observations are not trivial preliminaries to a more exciting religious explanation. They are the evidence against which an explanation must be tested. A missing feature should remain missing in the account rather than being supplied from an imagined complete figure.

The Harappa archive also preserves Daya Ram Sahni's report of figurines associated with smaller vessels inside a large jar. Such contextual information poses different questions from an isolated photograph. It can direct attention towards deposition and association without automatically explaining the ceremony, household activity or later disturbance that produced the arrangement.

The archive's discussion of Sharri R. Clark's research notes her challenge to an automatic “Mother Goddess” interpretation. The important change is methodological: representation, variation and context must be investigated rather than reduced to a single reproductive or sacred identity. This does not prove that no figurine had a religious role. It means that a religious role requires an argument.
Several questions can remain open together

For a hypothetical exhibition, compare three captions. “Mother Goddess” states an identity as settled. “Female figurine” describes an attribution based on representation but still needs attention to the surviving features. “Terracotta fragment with applied ornaments” may be more cautious where the evidence is incomplete. The most appropriate wording depends on the individual record; caution should sharpen description, not erase useful information.

Function is another question. A figure might have been handled, displayed or deposited in circumstances that are no longer recoverable. Size alone cannot decide whether it was a toy, a ritual object or something else. Nor can the presence of elaborate ornament establish a specific rank in an otherwise undocumented social hierarchy.

The pleasure of looking survives these limits. Clay carries decisions about proportion, attachment and expression that can be discussed without inventing a personal biography. An accurate account lets a visitor notice those decisions and follow the history of their interpretation. The object remains compelling because it has resisted complete explanation, not because a confident modern label has finally made it say more than the record supports.

title: Toy cart or ritual model? Reading miniature objects
summary: Miniature carts show how construction, context and revised identifications matter more than assuming that every small object was a toy.

body.text: A miniature cart immediately suggests movement. We imagine wheels turning and a hand pulling it across the ground. That response is understandable, but the imagination has already supplied a user and an activity. To study the object carefully, we need to return to its construction and the circumstances in which its parts were recovered.

The published Nausharo example provides unusually concrete information. The terracotta frame has openings interpreted as fittings for wooden elements, and two wheels were found beside it. The catalogue places the assemblage in Period III at Nausharo in Balochistan. Its proposed reconstruction depends on the arrangement of those features, not simply on a resemblance to a cart seen today.
A small structure with missing parts

This is an object whose surviving material does not necessarily represent its entire original construction. When a reconstruction adds wooden bars or an axle, it should distinguish the surviving terracotta from the inferred components. Colour-coding the additions or explaining them in a caption can make that distinction legible without making the display visually confusing.

The word “toy” in a catalogue is itself an interpretation worth understanding. A model capable of moving is compatible with play, but mechanical possibility and demonstrated use are not identical. Conversely, uncertainty should not prompt an equally unsupported ritual explanation. Calling a miniature sacred because its everyday use is unknown does not solve the evidential problem.

A second Harappa example shows how identifications can change. Daya Ram Sahni initially discussed curved, perforated terracotta pieces as possible implements for making twine, while acknowledging uncertainty. Kenoyer's later commentary identifies them as sides of miniature ox-carts. The archived record preserves both readings, allowing us to see that the present label emerged through comparison rather than appearing complete at excavation.
Reconstruction as a question

Imagine presenting a replica beside the documented fragments. Its usefulness would lie in showing how the proposed parts fit together. If the replica rolls, it demonstrates that this arrangement is mechanically possible. It does not prove who owned the ancient object, whether it was pulled often, or what stories accompanied its use. A demonstration tests one part of an interpretation, not an entire social history.

This makes miniatures especially good teaching objects. They bring design down to a scale where a visitor can follow connections and ask why an opening sits where it does. At the same time, their smallness encourages assumptions about children, domestic life and intention. Keeping the construction argument visible helps those appealing assumptions remain questions.

The best account therefore does not choose between a lifeless list of dimensions and an invented scene of ancient play. It connects the catalogue, the surviving parts and a clearly labelled reconstruction. The miniature becomes a record of making and a history of interpretation, while leaving its original users more room than a single confident story would allow.

title: Spindle whorls and the evidence for fibre work
summary: Spindle whorls are evidence for fibre work, but identifying a tool, a fibre and an ancient textile requires different observations.

body.text: A spindle whorl is an unassuming route into a largely missing world of cloth. The object helps a spindle turn while fibres are formed into thread. Its survival can draw attention to work that is less immediately visible than stone carving or metal casting, but a perforated object should not be assigned to spinning merely because that identification would complete a familiar story.

Rita Wright and colleagues' study of a jute textile trace from Harappa demonstrates the importance of combining different evidence. Their identification concerns material preserved on a ceramic object dated to the later third millennium BCE. They also discuss the possibility that some finds previously classified as wheels, weights or beads might have served as whorls. That is a research proposal, not a blanket relabelling of every pierced clay disc.
Tools and fibres answer different questions

The physical characteristics of a possible whorl can be recorded and compared, but a tool's presence does not automatically identify the fibre spun with it. The jute study relies on examination of the surviving textile structure for its material claim. A distinction between tool evidence and fibre evidence prevents a label from turning a plausible association into a demonstrated connection.

Jonathan Mark Kenoyer's survey of ancient Indus textiles describes the variety of indirect traces available, including impressions and fibres preserved in association with other materials. Such traces are fragmentary. A surviving scrap and a depiction of clothing do not offer identical information: one may preserve structure while the other presents a representation whose details require interpretation.

For a visitor, this opens a useful sequence of questions. Is the exhibit an actual fibre, an impression, a representation or a tool? What feature permits its identification? Does the evidence concern spinning, weaving or the finished garment? These distinctions make the subject more accessible because they show exactly how a claim has been reached.
Restoring labour without inventing a household

It is tempting to turn a whorl into a scene of a woman spinning in a named kind of household. Unless the context provides further evidence, that image adds gender, social organisation and location beyond what the object alone establishes. Recognising labour does not require assigning an anonymous worker a biography borrowed from another period.

A hypothetical display could instead place an accurately identified whorl beside a clearly labelled modern demonstration of spinning. The demonstration would explain the mechanism, while the ancient record would establish the find's identity and context. Its modern fibre and technique should remain explicit, so that an educational comparison does not quietly become a claim of exact continuity.

The whorl then tells a more demanding story than “people made cloth.” It introduces the difficulty of recovering ordinary work from uneven survival. It invites attention to the small traces through which skill becomes archaeologically visible, while reminding us that the absence of a complete textile is not permission to weave an unsupported one in words.

title: A cooking pot and its traces of use
summary: A pot’s form and its absorbed residues offer different evidence about food. Neither should be turned into a complete ancient recipe.

body.text: A vessel's shape can suggest how it might have been handled, filled or heated. It cannot, by itself, tell us everything that went inside. Calling an archaeological vessel a cooking pot is therefore the beginning of an investigation rather than a recovered menu. Surface traces, absorbed material and excavation context can each contribute different evidence.

Akshyeta Suryanarayan and collaborators analysed lipid residues in pottery from Indus settlements in present-day northwest India. Their study includes rural sites as well as larger settlements, rather than treating a single urban assemblage as representative of everyone. Its relevance to Pakistan's Indus heritage is comparative: these are not chemical results from a pot excavated at Harappa or Moenjodaro.
What remains inside the clay

The researchers identified evidence consistent with animal products, while explaining uncertainties in interpreting some chemical signatures. Mixtures and the lack of suitable local reference materials complicated particular assignments. This is a more careful result than a headline claiming to have recovered one universal Indus diet. Laboratory evidence can narrow possibilities without turning every sample into a named dish.

The distinction matters for public interpretation. A reference to dairy processing, for example, is not automatically evidence for a particular modern recipe. Nor does an ingredient category tell us the occasion, seasoning or social meaning of a meal. Those questions require additional evidence, and some may remain unanswered.

Experimental research offers another caution. A year-long cooking study compared different forms of residue to investigate whether they reflected a final use or accumulated cooking events. The key question is temporal: what interval of a vessel's history does a sample represent? A chemical trace need not be a direct snapshot of the last meal prepared before the pot was broken or abandoned.
Different clues, different scales

Imagine a museum display with a vessel drawing, a photograph of the sampled fragment and a summary of the analysis. Keeping them together would help visitors understand the chain from an excavated object to a scientific claim. The result should identify the actual sample, rather than illustrating an unrelated beautiful pot and allowing readers to assume it was tested.

This is also why a single vessel cannot stand in for a whole settlement's cuisine without qualification. People may have used different containers for different tasks, and the sampled material represents only what survived and was selected for analysis. A sensible account makes the limits of that selection part of the explanation instead of hiding them in technical notes.

The cooking pot is compelling precisely because it sits between ordinary life and analytical difficulty. We recognise the act of preparing food, yet its ancient details are not automatically familiar. Reading the vessel carefully means combining what its form permits, what its context records and what its residues support. The result is not a reconstructed dinner served with false certainty, but a better-founded encounter with past habits of nourishment and work.
